heart.caption: Blood makes a double loop: the right side pumps to the lungs, the left side to the body. At rest each beat moves about 70 mL, so roughly 5 L per minute from each ventricle.

right_atrium.caption: Right atrial pressure is only about 3 mmHg, the lowest in the heart. The small bump just before ventricular systole is the atrial kick.

left_atrium.caption: The atrium collects blood passively, then adds a small kick (the a wave) just before the ventricle contracts. Typical mean pressure is about 8 mmHg.

right_ventricle.caption: The right ventricle only has to push blood through the low-resistance lungs, so it peaks near 25 mmHg, about a fifth of the left side.

curves.x: s<1 ? ESV+(EDV-ESV)*s : s<2 ? EDV : s<3 ? EDV-(EDV-ESV)*(s-2) : ESV

left_ventricle.caption: The dot traces one beat on a pressure-volume loop: fill, squeeze with valves shut, eject, relax. The loop width is the stroke volume; normal ejection fraction is above 55%.

interventricular_septum.caption: The septum belongs to the thick left ventricle and bows toward the right. Wall thickness tracks workload: the left pumps against about 120 mmHg, the right only about 25.

tricuspid_valve.caption: The valve opens whenever atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure (filling) and slams shut when the ventricle squeezes. Watch where the curves cross.

mitral_valve.caption: The mitral valve is open only when left atrial pressure is above ventricular pressure. At the start of systole the ventricle overtakes the atrium and the valve closes (the first heart sound).

aortic_valve.caption: The aortic valve opens when the ventricle exceeds the aorta, about 80 mmHg, and shuts when it falls below (the second heart sound). A stiff or narrowed valve makes the ventricle work harder.

pulmonary_valve.caption: The pulmonary valve opens when right-ventricular pressure exceeds the pulmonary artery (about 10 mmHg at rest) and closes when it falls below it.

sa_node.caption: Each SA-node impulse starts a P wave (atria), then QRS (ventricles), then T (recovery). The node sets the rate: sympathetic nerves speed it up, vagal nerves slow it. Resting 60-100 bpm.

av_node.caption: The AV node holds the impulse back about 0.12-0.20 s (the PR interval), so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles squeeze. Drag the delay.

coronary_arteries.caption: Squeezing ventricular muscle clamps the coronary vessels, so most flow to the heart itself happens during diastole. Raise the heart rate and diastole (and flow time) shrinks.
coronary_arteries.xlabel: time (s)   |   y: mmHg  or  relative flow

aorta.caption: Mean pressure barely falls along the aorta and big arteries, then drops sharply across the arterioles, the main resistance. It is nearly zero by the time blood returns.

vena_cava.caption: Return flow to the heart is driven by the gap between mean systemic filling pressure and right atrial pressure. More blood volume (higher Pm) shifts it up; it plateaus when veins collapse below zero.
vena_cava.xlabel: right atrial pressure (mmHg)   |   y: venous return (L/min)

carotid_arteries.caption: Pressure sensors in the carotid sinus fire faster as pressure rises, telling the brainstem to slow the heart and widen vessels. Move the pressure and read the reflex.
carotid_arteries.xlabel: mean arterial pressure (mmHg)   |   y: firing (% of max)

artery.caption: Elastic arteries stretch with each beat and recoil between beats. Stiffer arteries (lower compliance, as with age) give a bigger pulse pressure for the same 70 mL stroke volume.

vein.caption: Thin, stretchy veins hold about two-thirds of your blood, so they act as a reservoir. Valves and the muscle pump push it uphill toward the heart.

capillary.caption: Along a capillary the pressure pushing fluid out falls from artery to vein while the protein pull stays near 25 mmHg, so fluid leaks out first and is drawn back at the end. Raise venous pressure and see swelling.
capillary.xlabel: artery end to vein end   |   y: mmHg

blood.caption: About 55% of blood is straw-coloured plasma and about 45% red cells. Slide the hematocrit to see how oxygen-carrying capacity follows it.

nose_airway.caption: Warm, moist mucosa heats and humidifies air so it reaches the lungs near body temperature and nearly 100% humidity. Cold air takes farther to warm up; slide the outside temperature.

larynx.caption: The vocal folds vibrate like a string: shorter or tighter folds give a higher pitch. Adult male folds are about 17-25 mm, female about 12-17 mm. Slide the tension.

trachea.caption: About 100 million cilia-covered cells sweep a mucus blanket up the airway (roughly 1 cm per minute), carrying trapped dust and germs to the throat. The C-shaped rings keep the tube open.

lung_l.caption: Air volume rises and falls with each breath around the resting level, about 2.4 L in an average adult man (Tortora, Principles of Anatomy and Physiology). Try deeper or faster breathing and watch minute ventilation change.

lung_l@woman.caption: Air volume rises and falls with each breath around the resting level, about 1.8 L in an average adult woman (Tortora, Principles of Anatomy and Physiology); not measured on this woman. Try deeper or faster breathing and watch minute ventilation change.

lung_r.caption: Air volume rises and falls with each breath around the resting level, about 2.4 L in an average adult man (Tortora, Principles of Anatomy and Physiology). Try deeper or faster breathing and watch minute ventilation change.

lung_r@woman.caption: Air volume rises and falls with each breath around the resting level, about 1.8 L in an average adult woman (Tortora, Principles of Anatomy and Physiology); not measured on this woman. Try deeper or faster breathing and watch minute ventilation change.

bronchi.caption: Each branching (generation) doubles the airway count. The tubes shrink, but the total cross-section grows from 2.5 cm² in the trachea to thousands of cm² at the end, so air slows to a crawl in the deep lung.
bronchi.xlabel: branching generation (0 = trachea)   |   y: log scale

bronchioles.caption: Resistance goes as 1 over radius to the fourth power, so a small narrowing (asthma, mucus) raises it a lot: halving the radius makes breathing 16 times harder. Slide the constriction.

alveoli.caption: Surface tension tries to collapse alveoli, and the pressure needed goes as 2T/r, worst for the smallest sacs. Surfactant slashes T so small and large alveoli can stay open together. Slide the tension.

diaphragm.caption: When the diaphragm contracts it flattens and pulls pleural pressure more negative, which drops alveolar pressure below atmospheric and draws air in. Quiet breathing moves it about 1.5 cm; deep breaths about 7 cm.

neuron.caption: Dendrites collect signals, the soma integrates them, and the axon sends a spike to terminals that release transmitter. The brain has about 86 billion such cells.

astrocyte.caption: Each star-shaped astrocyte touches thousands to hundreds of thousands of synapses with one set of arms and a capillary with its end-feet, passing nutrients to neurons and mopping up excess K+ and glutamate.

red_blood_cell.caption: Each biconcave red cell (7.5 µm wide, about 270 million hemoglobins) loads oxygen in the lungs (PO2 about 100) and unloads it in tissue (about 40). Acid, CO2 or heat shift the curve right so more O2 is released; try it.

neutrophil.caption: Neutrophils (about 60% of white cells, 10-12 µm, multilobed nucleus) arrive first at an infection, within an hour, following chemical trails and killing germs with enzymes and reactive oxygen. They live only about a day.

macrophage.caption: Macrophages are the clean-up and alarm cells: they digest what they swallow, then display fragments on their surface so T cells can recognise the invader. They can live for months.

lymphocyte_t.caption: A T cell is activated only when its receptor recognises a matching fragment shown on another cell. It then becomes a helper that directs the response (cytokines), a killer that destroys infected cells, or a long-lived memory cell.

lymphocyte_b.caption: A B cell that meets its antigen turns into a plasma cell: an antibody factory pumping out about 2,000 antibody molecules per second. Some daughters stay behind as memory cells for a faster second response.

platelet.caption: A platelet is a cell fragment (150-450 billion per litre of blood, lifespan 8-10 days). Slide activation to see the resting disc turn into the spiky, sticky form that plugs a wound.

cardiomyocyte.caption: Unlike a nerve spike (about 2 ms), the heart-cell action potential has a 200-300 ms plateau held up by calcium entry. The plateau makes the contraction long (dashed) and prevents tetanus, so the heart can refill.

skeletal_muscle_fiber.caption: A fiber is strongest near its resting sarcomere length of about 2.2 µm, where thick and thin filaments overlap best. Stretched or squashed too far, they cannot pull. Slide the length.

smooth_muscle_cell.caption: Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped (about 5 µm wide, 200 µm long). They contract by a chemical cascade rather than the rapid trigger of skeletal muscle, which lets them hold tension for long periods at low energy cost.

hepatocyte.caption: Hepatocytes make up about 80% of the liver and carry out hundreds of jobs, including making 0.5-1 L of bile a day and about 10-15 g of albumin. Blood flows past them in sinusoids, bringing nutrients and carrying products away.

enterocyte.caption: Nutrients are taken up across the brush border (a sodium-linked transporter pulls glucose in) and leave through the cell base into the blood. Tight junctions keep the gut contents out.

osteocyte.caption: Osteocytes make up about 90-95% of bone cells. Each sits in a tiny cavity and reaches neighbours through thin channels, acting as the bone's strain sensors that tell it where to add or remove material.

osteoblast.caption: Osteoblasts build bone: they lay down collagen and then trigger mineral (hydroxyapatite) crystals to form. About 10-20% become buried as osteocytes.

osteoclast.caption: Osteoclasts are large, multinucleated cells that dissolve bone: acid removes the mineral and enzymes (cathepsin K) digest the collagen. They work together with osteoblasts to renew the skeleton.

chondrocyte.caption: Cartilage has no blood vessels, so its cells (chondrocytes) feed by diffusion from joint fluid, and movement pumps fluid through the matrix. That is why cartilage heals slowly.

keratinocyte.caption: Keratinocytes make up about 90% of the epidermis. They are born at the base, fill with keratin and die as they climb to the surface over roughly four weeks, where they form the waterproof outer layer.

adipocyte.caption: A fat cell stores energy as a single droplet that can fill nearly the whole cell (about 90% fat). Fill it from empty to full: the cell swells from about 40 to over 100 µm, a 15-fold volume change.

fibroblast.caption: Fibroblasts are the connective-tissue builders: after an injury they multiply, lay down collagen and pull the wound edges together. Too much activity leaves a scar.

rod_cell.caption: Walk from sunlight into a dark room: cones adapt first, then at about 7-10 minutes the rods take over and sensitivity keeps improving for 30 minutes or more (the lower the curve, the dimmer the light you can detect).
rod_cell.xlabel: minutes in the dark   |   y: detection threshold (log units)

cone_cell.caption: Three cone types, each peaking at a different wavelength, let the brain compare their responses to see color. Rods (dashed) peak near 498 nm and give no color. Slide the wavelength.

sperm.caption: A sperm is a swimmer: the head carries half a set of chromosomes (and an enzyme cap, the acrosome), the midpiece's mitochondria power the tail, which beats about 10-15 times a second to reach about 3 mm per minute.

egg_cell.caption: The egg is about 0.12 mm across, visible to the naked eye, and wrapped in layers. A sperm must cross the helper cells and zona; contact triggers the cortical granules to harden the coat so only one sperm enters.

stem_cell.caption: One blood stem cell in the bone marrow can renew itself and give rise to every blood cell type, via myeloid progenitors (red cells, platelets, neutrophils...) or lymphoid ones. The body makes roughly 200 billion red cells every day this way.

melanocyte.caption: A melanocyte (about 1 for every 36 basal keratinocytes) makes pigment in packets and hands it to its neighbours, which place it above their nuclei like tiny umbrellas. Skin colour depends on how much and what type of melanin, not on the number of melanocytes.

beta_cell.caption: Beta cells sense glucose directly: more glucose means more ATP inside, which closes K+ channels, opens calcium channels and releases insulin. Secretion switches on steeply above the fasting level of about 5 mM. Slide the blood glucose.

blood_vessels.caption: Same flow, different total cross-section: blood speed = flow / area, so it crawls through the huge capillary bed, giving time for exchange. Raise cardiac output to speed everything up.

synapse.caption: Vesicles in the sending terminal release transmitter (gold dots) across the tiny gap, where it binds receptors (green) on the receiving cell. The cleft is only about 20 nm wide, so crossing takes under a millisecond.

neuromuscular_junction.caption: One motor-neuron spike releases acetylcholine and produces an end-plate potential about 3-4 times bigger than needed to fire the muscle. In myasthenia gravis receptors are lost: slide the receptors down until it fails.

tendon.caption: Pull a tendon: first the crimped collagen straightens (flat toe), then it stiffens (a stiffness of about 1 GPa) and fails near 10% strain at about 100 MPa. Drag the strain; tendons store and return elastic energy.

pectoralis_major.caption: The pectoralis major pulls the arm forward and across the chest, as in a push-up or throw. Drag the arm forward to see the muscle shorten.

deltoid.caption: The deltoid lifts the arm out to the side (abduction). Its leverage changes as the arm rises; watch the moment arm and torque readouts.

biceps_brachii.caption: The biceps pulls the forearm up (flexion). Its leverage is greatest near a right angle, about 3.5-4 cm. A 600 N pull gives roughly 20 N·m of elbow torque. Drag the elbow angle and the force.

triceps_brachii.caption: The triceps lies behind the elbow and straightens it. As you bend the elbow the muscle is stretched; drag the angle to see its length and leverage change.

rectus_abdominis.caption: The strap-like rectus abdominis lies in front of the spine and curls the trunk forward (a sit-up). It is far from the pivot, so it has a long lever arm of about 10 cm.

external_obliques.caption: The external obliques run diagonally along the side of the trunk. One side alone bends the trunk to that side; both together flex it, and diagonal pairs twist it. Side view simplified.

quadriceps.caption: The four quadriceps heads straighten the knee through the patella and patellar tendon. Bend the knee: the muscle stretches. Raise the force to see how the knee torque grows.

hamstrings.caption: The hamstrings run behind the knee: they bend it and extend the hip. Flex the knee and the muscle shortens, which is why they cramp easily at full shortening.

gastrocnemius.caption: The calf muscle pulls on the heel through the Achilles tendon and points the foot (plantarflexion), as in a heel raise. A 3000 N pull on a 5 cm lever gives about 150 N·m.

gluteus_maximus.caption: The gluteus maximus is the body's biggest muscle and the main hip extensor, used in climbing and sprinting. Flexing the hip (lifting the thigh forward) stretches it.

trapezius.caption: The upper trapezius tilts the head backward (and raises the shoulder). Move the head back: the muscle shortens and its moment arm changes.

latissimus_dorsi.caption: The latissimus pulls the raised arm down and back, as in a pull-up or rowing. Swing the arm backward (extension) and watch the muscle shorten.

sternocleidomastoid.caption: The two sternocleidomastoids bend the head forward; one alone turns and tilts it. Drag the nod angle to see it shorten.

brain.caption: The brain is only about 2% of body weight yet uses about 20% of the body's resting energy and oxygen and about 15% of blood flow, which is why it fails within seconds without blood.

frontal_lobe.caption: Seen from the left: the frontal lobe (cyan) is the largest, about a third of the cortex, and handles planning, decisions, speech production and voluntary movement through the motor strip at its back edge.

parietal_lobe.caption: The parietal lobe (gold) sits behind the central sulcus: it receives touch and body-position signals and builds your sense of where things are in space.

temporal_lobe.caption: The temporal lobe (green) lies below the lateral sulcus, next to the ears: hearing, understanding language, and (deep inside) memory.

occipital_lobe.caption: The occipital lobe (pink) at the back is dominated by the primary visual cortex; damage here can cause blindness even with healthy eyes.

cerebral_cortex.caption: Folding packs a large sheet (about 2,400 cm², 2-4 mm thick) into the skull. Surface area grows much faster than brain volume across species (approximate values).

hippocampus.caption: A new memory fades unless the hippocampus helps consolidate it. Each rehearsal (spaced review) slows the forgetting curve. Add reviews and compare.

hypothalamus.caption: The hypothalamus holds temperature near 37 °C, but its internal clock lets it swing about 0.5 °C a day: lowest around 5 am, highest in the early evening.

corpus_callosum.caption: The corpus callosum is a bundle of about 200 million fibers that lets the two hemispheres share information. Each half of the visual field is processed by the opposite hemisphere, so the callosum is needed to join the picture.

thalamus.caption: Almost every sense passes through the thalamus on its way to the cortex, like a switchboard that also gates attention. Smell is the exception: it reaches the cortex directly.

amygdala.caption: A fast route sends a crude alert straight from the thalamus to the amygdala, before the cortex has finished identifying the object; the slower cortical route can then confirm or cancel the alarm.

basal_ganglia.caption: The basal ganglia hold a constant brake on movement. When the striatum lifts the brake (by inhibiting the GPi), the thalamus is freed and the cortex can act. Dopamine loss, as in Parkinson disease, makes starting movement hard.

cerebellum.caption: The cerebellum holds about 80% of the brain's neurons. It compares the intended movement with sensory feedback of what actually happened and sends corrections within milliseconds, making movements smooth.

brainstem.caption: The brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla) runs automatic life-support jobs (breathing 12-20 per minute, heart rate, blood pressure) and is the cable through which every signal between brain and body passes. Damage here is quickly life-threatening.

spinal_cord.caption: In a reflex, such as the knee jerk, the signal turns around in the spinal cord and never waits for the brain, so the response takes only about 30-50 ms.

peripheral_nerves.caption: Fatter axons conduct faster, and myelin (insulation) multiplies the speed: big myelinated fibers reach about 100 m/s, thin unmyelinated pain fibers only 1-2 m/s.

eye_l.caption: Light is bent mostly by the cornea (about 43 D) and fine-tuned by the lens (about 17-30 D), passes the pupil, crosses the vitreous gel and lands on the retina, which sends signals down the optic nerve.

eye_r.caption: Light is bent mostly by the cornea (about 43 D) and fine-tuned by the lens (about 17-30 D), passes the pupil, crosses the vitreous gel and lands on the retina, which sends signals down the optic nerve.

cornea.caption: The cornea does about two-thirds of the eye's focusing (about 43 diopters of roughly 60), because light bends most where it enters from air. The lens adds the adjustable remainder.

iris.caption: The iris widens the pupil to about 8 mm in the dark and shrinks it to 2 mm in bright light, changing the light let in by up to 16 times. Slide the brightness.
iris.xlabel: scene luminance (cd/m², log scale)   |   y: mm

lens.caption: Focusing near means squeezing the lens fatter. With age the lens stiffens, so the range falls from about 15 diopters in a child to nearly zero by 55-60 (presbyopia). Slide age.

vitreous_humor.caption: The clear vitreous gel is 98-99% water and fills about 80% of the eye, about 4 mL, holding the retina against the back of the eye and keeping the eyeball round.

retina.caption: Cones (color, detail) crowd into the center, the fovea; rods (dim light) peak about 18 degrees away and are absent from the fovea. That is why a faint star vanishes when you look straight at it.
retina.xlabel: angle from the fovea (°)   |   y: cells per mm²

fovea.caption: Sharp vision lives in a tiny pit about 1.5 mm wide. Acuity falls to half at only 2 degrees (about the width of your thumbnail at arm's length) and is poor in the periphery. Slide the angle.
fovea.xlabel: angle from the point you look at (°)   |   y: % of best

optic_nerve.caption: The optic nerve carries about 1 million fibers from each eye to the thalamus (LGN) and on to visual cortex V1. At the chiasm the inner (nasal) half of each retina crosses over, so each hemisphere sees the opposite half of the world.

nucleus.caption: A human cell's DNA is about 2 m long (6 billion base pairs) but is coiled around histones into a nucleus only 6 µm wide: a compaction of about 300,000 times.

shapes.text: ATP synthase (gold) turns the proton flow into ATP

mitochondrion.caption: The electron-transport chain pumps protons across the inner membrane; their return flow through ATP synthase makes about 90% of the cell's ATP (roughly 26-28 of the ~30 per glucose). Folding into cristae increases the area.

ribosome.caption: A ribosome adds amino acids one at a time (about 5 per second in human cells, 20 in bacteria). An average 400-amino-acid protein takes about 80 seconds; the 34,000-amino-acid giant titin takes about two hours.
ribosome.xlabel: protein length (amino acids)   |   y: minutes to build

endoplasmic_reticulum.caption: The rough ER (studded with ribosomes) makes proteins for export and membranes; the smooth ER makes lipids and stores calcium. About a third of all proteins pass through it.

golgi_apparatus.caption: The Golgi is the cell's post office: proteins are tagged with sugars and address labels as they move through the stack, then packaged in vesicles bound for the membrane, lysosomes or secretion.

lysosome.caption: Lysosomal enzymes work only in strong acid (pH 4.5-5, about 300 times more H+ than the cytosol at pH 7.2), so a leak is mostly harmless to the rest of the cell. pH values: cytosol 7.2, endosome 6, lysosome 4.7, stomach 1.5. H+ concentration, log scale.

peroxisome.caption: Peroxisomes break down very long fatty acids and some toxins. They make hydrogen peroxide as a by-product, then safely split it with catalase, one of the fastest enzymes known (millions of reactions per second).

cell_membrane.caption: The membrane voltage comes from unequal ion concentrations and selective leaks. Outside K+ is normally about 4 mM; raise it (hyperkalemia) and the cell depolarizes. More Na+ leak (higher b) also pulls it toward zero.

cytoskeleton.caption: Three filament systems give a cell its shape: thin actin (7 nm) for movement and the cell cortex, ropelike intermediate filaments (10 nm) for strength, and hollow microtubules (25 nm) that act as rails for motor proteins moving cargo at about 1 µm per second.

shapes.text: myosin (thick) pulls actin (thin) toward the center

sarcomere.caption: Filaments do not shorten; they slide. Z discs (white) are pulled together as myosin heads walk along actin, so the sarcomere shortens from about 2.6 to 1.8 µm. Thousands in a row make a muscle shorten.

cardiac_cycle.caption: Ventricular pressure shoots past aortic pressure to open the valve (systole), then falls below it so the valve shuts. Raise the heart rate: diastole shrinks most.

breathing.caption: Red cells pick up oxygen within about a quarter of a second of their 0.75 s trip past an alveolus, leaving a safety margin. Thicken the barrier (disease) or shorten the transit time (hard exercise) and the margin shrinks.
breathing.xlabel: time in the capillary (s)   |   y: PO2 (mmHg)

action_potential.caption: A stimulus that lifts the voltage above threshold (about -55 mV) triggers a full spike to about +30 mV and an undershoot; a weaker one just fades. This is the all-or-none rule. Slide the stimulus.

synaptic_transmission.caption: The whole chemical hop takes only about 0.5-1 ms. Calcium entry is the trigger: block it and the signal stops. Cleaning up the transmitter afterwards resets the synapse.

muscle_contraction.caption: Each cycle moves the thin filament about 10 nm and costs one ATP. A muscle runs this cycle in millions of heads at once. Without ATP the heads stay locked (rigor mortis).

digestion.caption: Food spends seconds in the mouth, 2-4 hours in the stomach, 3-5 hours in the small intestine (where nearly all nutrients are absorbed) and 12-48 hours in the colon, which recovers water. The whole tube is about 9 m long.

urine_formation.caption: Each day the kidneys filter about 180 litres of plasma but excrete only about 1.5 litres: over 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed. Most is reclaimed in the first tube; hormones fine-tune the rest.

blood_clotting.caption: Clotting is a chain reaction in which each activated factor activates the next, so a tiny trigger is amplified into a solid fibrin mesh within minutes. Normal bleeding stops in about 2-9 minutes. Plasmin dissolves the clot after healing.

immune_response.caption: The first meeting with a germ takes about a week to produce a modest antibody peak. Memory cells let a second exposure (day D) respond within days and produce 10-100 times as much. Slide the booster day.

hormone_signaling.caption: After a meal glucose rises, beta cells release insulin, and the falling glucose switches the release off: negative feedback. If tissues respond poorly (low sensitivity, as in type 2 diabetes) glucose peaks higher and stays up longer. Slide sensitivity.
hormone_signaling.xlabel: hours after a meal   |   y: mg/dL

cellular_respiration.caption: Burning one glucose with oxygen yields about 30 ATP, 15 times more than glycolysis alone. Cut off the oxygen and the cell is left with just the 2 ATP from glycolysis.

protein_synthesis.caption: DNA is copied to mRNA (about 50 bases per second), then a ribosome reads it three bases at a time, adding one amino acid per codon (about 5 per second).

mitosis.caption: Mitosis itself takes only about an hour of a roughly 24-hour cell cycle. Each daughter cell receives an identical set of 46 chromosomes.

bone_remodeling.caption: About 10% of bone is replaced every year, so the whole skeleton is renewed roughly every 10 years. Dissolving is quick and rebuilding slow; if the two get out of balance, bone is lost (osteoporosis).

vision.caption: Unusually, a photoreceptor is active in the dark and switches off in light: one photon can eventually close hundreds of channels, which makes the rod able to detect a single photon.

thermoregulation.caption: Temperature is held near 37 °C by negative feedback: sensors in skin and brain report to the hypothalamus, which compares with its set point and switches on heating (shiver, narrow skin vessels) if too cold or cooling (sweat, wide vessels) if too hot, until the error disappears.

skull.caption: The skull has 22 bones (8 cranial, 14 facial) fused by immovable sutures, except the mandible. Each ear also holds three tiny ossicles (6 in total), the smallest bones in the body.

mandible.caption: The jaw is a lever with the pivot (joint) at one end and the muscles close to it, so biting is strongest at the back teeth and weakest at the front. Move the tooth position or the muscle force.
mandible.xlabel: distance from jaw joint (cm)   |   y: bite force (N)

cervical_spine.caption: Seven small vertebrae make the neck the most mobile part of the spine. The top two (atlas and axis) alone give about half of the head's rotation. Typical range in each direction, degrees.

thoracic_spine.caption: The 12 thoracic vertebrae carry the ribs. The rib cage stiffens this part of the spine for bending, but allows about 35° of twist to each side, more than the lumbar spine. Rotation to one side by region.

lumbar_spine.caption: The five lumbar vertebrae carry most of the body's weight, and the pressure inside the discs depends on posture. Lifting with a bent back loads the discs nearly three times as much as standing (standing = 100).

sacrum.caption: The sacrum is five vertebrae fused into one wedge, wedged between the hip bones; with the coccyx (3-5 fused) it ends the 33 vertebrae of the spine. Number of vertebrae per region.

ribcage.caption: Seen from above (a horizontal slice), breathing in swings the ribs up and out like bucket handles: the chest grows front-to-back and side-to-side, and the lungs expand into the extra space.

sternum.caption: The breastbone (about 17 cm) has three parts. In CPR the rescuer presses the body of the sternum about 5-6 cm to squeeze the heart. Typical length of each part.

pelvis.caption: The pelvic ring carries upper-body weight down into the legs and also protects the pelvic organs. Weight flows from the spine through the sacrum and sacroiliac joints to the hip bones, then out through the hip sockets to the femurs.

clavicle_l.caption: The collarbone is the only bony strut linking the arm to the trunk. It holds the shoulder out to the side and passes forces from the arm to the chest, which is why falls on an outstretched hand often break it.

scapula_l.caption: Raising the arm overhead is shared: about 2° at the shoulder joint for every 1° the blade rotates on the back. Drag the arm angle to see the split.

humerus_l.caption: The humerus is about 19% of body height (about 32 cm in a 170 cm adult). The ratios are stable enough that forensic scientists estimate height from a single long bone. Slide the height.

radius_ulna_l.caption: The radius is about 14.5% of body height. The forearm bones cross over each other (pronation), letting you turn the palm up or down without moving the elbow. Slide the height.

hand_bones_l.caption: Each hand holds 27 bones (8 carpals in the wrist, 5 metacarpals in the palm, 14 phalanges in the fingers), a quarter of all the bones in the body for only about 2% of its mass: the price of fine dexterity.

femur_l.caption: The femur's head carries the whole upper body through the hip. The joint force is several times body weight in everyday movement (the muscles add to it): about 3 times in walking and 5 or more in running. Slide the body mass.

fns.label: force on kneecap joint (x body weight)

patella_l.caption: The kneecap shifts the quadriceps pull forward, increasing its leverage, but the squeeze on the joint behind it grows steeply with knee bend: about 0.4 body weight at 30°, about 3 at 90° in a squat (approximate). Drag the angle.
patella_l.xlabel: knee bend (°)   |   y: x body weight

tibia_fibula_l.caption: The weight-bearing tibia is about 22% of body height; the slim fibula carries only about 6-17% of the load. Forensic estimates of stature use these ratios. Slide the height.

foot_bones_l.caption: Each foot has 26 bones (7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges) arranged in arches that act as springs, storing and returning about 17% of the energy of each running stride.

clavicle_r.caption: The collarbone is the only bony strut linking the arm to the trunk. It holds the shoulder out to the side and passes forces from the arm to the chest, which is why falls on an outstretched hand often break it.

scapula_r.caption: Raising the arm overhead is shared: about 2° at the shoulder joint for every 1° the blade rotates on the back. Drag the arm angle to see the split.

humerus_r.caption: The humerus is about 19% of body height (about 32 cm in a 170 cm adult). The ratios are stable enough that forensic scientists estimate height from a single long bone. Slide the height.

radius_ulna_r.caption: The radius is about 14.5% of body height. The forearm bones cross over each other (pronation), letting you turn the palm up or down without moving the elbow. Slide the height.

hand_bones_r.caption: Each hand holds 27 bones (8 carpals in the wrist, 5 metacarpals in the palm, 14 phalanges in the fingers), a quarter of all the bones in the body for only about 2% of its mass: the price of fine dexterity.

femur_r.caption: The femur's head carries the whole upper body through the hip. The joint force is several times body weight in everyday movement (the muscles add to it): about 3 times in walking and 5 or more in running. Slide the body mass.

fns.label: force on kneecap joint (x body weight)

patella_r.caption: The kneecap shifts the quadriceps pull forward, increasing its leverage, but the squeeze on the joint behind it grows steeply with knee bend: about 0.4 body weight at 30°, about 3 at 90° in a squat (approximate). Drag the angle.
patella_r.xlabel: knee bend (°)   |   y: x body weight

tibia_fibula_r.caption: The weight-bearing tibia is about 22% of body height; the slim fibula carries only about 6-17% of the load. Forensic estimates of stature use these ratios. Slide the height.

foot_bones_r.caption: Each foot has 26 bones (7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges) arranged in arches that act as springs, storing and returning about 17% of the energy of each running stride.

long_bone.caption: A long bone is a light, strong tube: a hard shell of compact bone around a marrow cavity in the shaft, with spongy bone at the ends and a cartilage cap where it forms a joint. The dashed lines are growth plates.

compact_bone.caption: Compact bone (gold) resists crushing nearly as well as steel (170 MPa vs about 250) at a quarter of the weight, thanks to its mineral-and-collagen composite. Typical compressive strength, log scale.

spongy_bone.caption: Spongy bone is a lattice with a density of only 0.2-0.8 g/cm³ versus 1.9 for compact bone, yet its strength rises with the square of the density. Doubling the density quadruples its strength. Slide the density.

bone_marrow.caption: Red marrow produces roughly 200 billion red cells, 100 billion platelets and 100 billion neutrophils every day (about 5 million new cells per second). Approximate daily production, log scale.

periosteum.caption: The periosteum is the bone's skin: its tough outer layer anchors tendons and carries nerves (why a bone bruise hurts) and its inner layer holds cells that build new bone, which also lets a broken bone heal.

growth_plate.caption: A cartilage plate near each end of the bone keeps adding length until hormones at the end of puberty turn it to bone. Growth is fast in infancy, then settles to about 5-6 cm a year, with a puberty spurt of 8-10 cm. Slide the spurt age.

synovial_joint.caption: Lubricated by synovial fluid, cartilage slides against cartilage with a friction coefficient of about 0.01, slicker than ice. Healthy joints can last 80 years of walking. Log scale.

human_body.caption: An adult body is about 60% water by mass, with the rest mostly protein, fat and the mineral of bone, built from about 30 trillion human cells (and a similar number of microbes). Fat is the variable part: slide it and the water share changes.

integumentary_system.caption: The skin covers about 1.8 m² and makes up about 15% of body weight. It keeps water in and germs out, regulates temperature, makes vitamin D from sunlight and houses touch sensors.

skeletal_system.caption: Adults have 206 bones: 80 in the axial skeleton (skull, spine, chest) and 126 in the limbs. Babies are born with about 300, which fuse as they grow. Bones also store 99% of the body's calcium and make blood cells.

muscular_system.caption: About 600 skeletal muscles make up about 40% of body mass. They turn chemical energy into force but only about 25% efficiently; the rest becomes heat that keeps us warm. A nerve signal triggers each contraction.

nervous_system.caption: The nervous system gathers sensory data, integrates it in the brain and spinal cord, and sends commands to muscles, organs (autonomic nerves) and glands, in milliseconds. About 86 billion neurons and 100 trillion synapses carry out this work.

endocrine_system.caption: Endocrine glands send chemical messengers (hormones) through the blood to far-off target organs. The hypothalamus and pituitary form the control center, and most axes run on negative feedback.

cardiovascular_system.caption: A closed loop of about 100,000 km of vessels: the heart pumps oxygen-rich blood through arteries to capillaries, where exchange happens, and veins return it; a second loop through the lungs picks up fresh oxygen. Cardiac output is about 5 L/min.

lymphatic_immune_system.caption: Lymph vessels return about 3 L of leaked fluid a day to the blood, passing through lymph nodes where immune cells inspect it. Bone marrow makes the immune cells, the thymus trains T cells, and the spleen filters blood and samples it for germs.

respiratory_system.caption: About 12-20 breaths a minute move about 6 L of air in and out. In the 300-500 million alveoli (a surface of about 70 m²), oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it, powered by the diaphragm.

digestive_system.caption: The 9 m digestive tube breaks food down and absorbs nutrients (mostly in the small intestine), helped by bile from the liver and enzymes from the pancreas; the colon recovers water.

urinary_system.caption: The kidneys clean the blood (about 1.2 L a minute in, about 180 L of filtrate a day), keep water, salts and acidity in balance and pass about 1.5 L of urine to the bladder through the ureters.

reproductive_system.caption: The reproductive organs are run by a brain-gonad hormone loop (GnRH, then LH and FSH, then testosterone or estrogen and progesterone, with feedback to the brain). They make the gametes, and in females the uterus supports an embryo for about 38 weeks.

epithelial_tissue.caption: Epithelia are named by cell shape (flat squamous, cube-shaped, tall columnar) and layers (simple = one, stratified = many). The structure matches the job: thin for exchange (lung), absorbing (gut), tough for protection (skin), stretchy (bladder). They have no blood vessels and are renewed quickly.

connective_tissue_loose.caption: Loose connective tissue is the body's packing material under skin and around organs: sparse fibers and cells floating in a gel. It supports vessels and nerves and is the first place an infection meets immune cells.

dense_connective_tissue.caption: Dense connective tissue is packed with parallel collagen, a rope-like protein: about 70-85% of its dry weight. That is why tendons and ligaments are so strong but poorly stretchy and heal slowly. Approximate collagen share of dry weight.

adipose_tissue.caption: Fat stores about 9 kcal per gram, over twice as much as carbohydrate, and a lean adult carries about 100,000 kcal of it (more than 50 days of fasting) versus only about 2,000 kcal as glycogen. Slide the fat mass. Log scale.

cartilage_tissue.caption: Cartilage is a squishy gel: under steady load water slowly squeezes out and it compresses by about 10-15%, recovering when unloaded. This is why we are about 1 cm shorter at night and why cartilage needs movement to be nourished. Slide the load.

bone_tissue.caption: Compact bone is built from osteons: concentric layers (lamellae) of mineralised collagen wrapped around a central canal that carries blood, with osteocytes in tiny cavities linked by channels. The layered tube resists cracking.

blood_tissue.caption: In each microliter of blood there are about 5 million red cells, 250,000 platelets and only about 7,000 white cells in several types. Typical adult counts per µL, log scale.

skeletal_muscle_tissue.caption: Muscle is organised in nested bundles, each wrapped in connective tissue, down to the molecular filaments. A single fibre can be 10 cm long and contain 100s of nuclei; a muscle shortens when about 100 billion sarcomeres shorten together.

cardiac_muscle_tissue.caption: Heart muscle cells are joined end to end by intercalated discs, so an impulse spreads through them like one unit. Slow conduction through the AV node gives the atria time to empty; fast Purkinje fibers then fire the ventricle all at once. Speed in m/s, log scale.

smooth_muscle_tissue.caption: Smooth muscle contracts about 100 times more slowly than skeletal muscle but can hold tension for minutes at very little energy cost, ideal for vessel walls and the gut. The time axis is logarithmic.
smooth_muscle_tissue.xlabel: time after stimulus (s)   |   y: relative force

nervous_tissue.caption: The brain has about 86 billion neurons and about the same number of supporting glial cells (not the 10:1 once taught). Neurons do the signaling; glia insulate, feed and protect them. Billions of cells.

simple_squamous_epithelium.caption: Diffusion time grows with the square of distance (t = x²/2D), so exchange surfaces must be very thin: the alveolar-capillary barrier is only about 0.5 µm and gases cross in milliseconds, while 1 mm would take minutes. Slide the distance.

simple_columnar_epithelium.caption: Tall columnar cells are polarised: one side (the top) has transporters that take up nutrients, and the other side exports them. Tight junctions between cells keep the gut contents out, and goblet cells add protective mucus.

stratified_squamous_epithelium.caption: Many layers protect against wear: the base cells divide and push older cells upward, where they flatten and lose their nuclei. Skin, mouth, esophagus and vagina use this design, so scrapes are replaced from below.

transitional_epithelium.caption: The bladder lining adapts to being empty or full. Slide the filling: when stretched the dome-shaped surface cells flatten and spread, and the layers thin from about 6 cell layers to 2-3, without tearing or leaking.

mouth_pharynx.caption: Swallowing is a reflex that takes about a second in the throat. The airway is briefly shut (breathing pauses) so food goes down the esophagus, not the windpipe.

esophagus.caption: A ring of squeeze (about 3-4 cm per second) pushes each swallow down the 25 cm tube, so you can swallow even upside down. The sphincter at the bottom (right) relaxes just as the wave arrives.
esophagus.xlabel: distance down the esophagus (cm)   |   y: mmHg

stomach.caption: Liquids leave the stomach within about 20 minutes, but a solid meal is ground into a paste first (the lag) and then emptied in small squirts over 3-4 hours. Fatty meals slow it further. Slide the lag.
stomach.xlabel: hours after eating   |   y: % still in stomach

gastric_pits.caption: Parietal cells pump out acid (about 2 L of juice a day, pH 1.5-2) that is strong enough to dissolve metal. A mucus layer of about 0.2 mm, rich in bicarbonate, holds the pH near neutral at the cells so the stomach does not digest itself.
gastric_pits.xlabel: distance from the stomach cavity to the cell wall (µm)   |   y: pH

small_intestine.caption: About 9 litres of fluid (2 drunk plus 7 from the body's own juices) enter the gut each day, and the small intestine takes back about 7.5 of them along with nearly all nutrients. Only about 100 mL leaves in stool.

villi.caption: Each villus (about 1 mm tall, 20-40 per mm²) has a capillary for water-soluble nutrients (sugars, amino acids, which go to the liver by the portal vein) and a lymph vessel, the lacteal, for fat. Villi and microvilli together multiply the absorbing surface about 600-fold.

large_intestine.caption: The colon is slow: food waste takes about 12-48 hours (30-40 on average) to cross it while water and salts are absorbed and gut bacteria ferment fibre. Typical transit time in each region.

microbiome.caption: Bacteria thrive in the oxygen-poor colon: about 100 billion per millilitre, tens of trillions in total (roughly as many as human cells). Acid and fast flow keep numbers low upstream. Log scale.

liver.caption: The liver gets 1.5 L of blood a minute from two sources: nutrient-rich, oxygen-poor blood from the gut (portal vein, 75%) and oxygen-rich arterial blood (25%). It handles everything absorbed from food, makes 0.6-1 L of bile a day and plasma proteins, and detoxifies.

shapes.text: portal triads at the corners (artery, vein, bile duct)
blood flows corner to center through sinusoids

liver_lobule.caption: The hexagonal lobule is the liver's working unit: blood runs from the corner triads, past rows of hepatocytes, to the central vein, so cells near the corners get the most oxygen and nutrients (zone 1) and those near the center the least.

gallbladder.caption: The gallbladder stores bile (concentrating it 5-10 times, 30-50 mL). A fatty meal releases the hormone CCK, which squeezes out about 60-70% of it within an hour; then it refills. Slide the ejection fraction.
gallbladder.xlabel: minutes after a fatty meal   |   y: mL

pancreas.caption: About 98% of the pancreas is exocrine: acinar cells send 1-1.5 L a day of digestive enzymes and bicarbonate to the gut by a duct. The remaining 1-2%, in islets, is endocrine: insulin and glucagon go into the blood to control glucose.

pancreatic_islets.caption: A human has about a million islets, each with about 1,000 cells. Beta cells (insulin, lowers glucose) are the majority, and alpha cells (glucagon, raises glucose) are their opposite. Approximate share of islet cells.

kidney_l.caption: Kidneys receive about 1.2 L of blood per minute (a fifth of the output) and keep flow and filtration almost constant for pressures from about 80 to 180 mmHg (autoregulation), protecting the filters from swings. Move the pressure.

kidney_r.caption: Kidneys receive about 1.2 L of blood per minute (a fifth of the output) and keep flow and filtration almost constant for pressures from about 80 to 180 mmHg (autoregulation), protecting the filters from swings. Move the pressure.

renal_cortex.caption: The outer cortex holds the million glomerular filters and receives about 90% of the kidney's blood flow. The deeper medulla gets much less, which helps it keep its salt gradient. Share of renal blood flow.

renal_medulla.caption: The medulla is saltier the deeper you go: from blood-like 300 mOsm/kg at the cortex to about 1200 at the tip. Water is drawn out of urine into this gradient, which is how we make urine four times more concentrated than blood. Slide the depth.
renal_medulla.xlabel: depth in the medulla (0 = cortex, 1 = papilla tip)   |   y: mOsm/kg

renal_pelvis.caption: Urine drains from about 10-18 minor calyces, which merge into 2-3 major calyces and then into the funnel-shaped renal pelvis. Waves of squeezing push it on to the ureter a few times per minute.

nephron.caption: Percentage of filtered water remaining along the tubule: 65% is reclaimed in the first tube, more in the loop and distal tube, and the collecting duct makes the final decision under control of the hormone ADH. Slide ADH to see urine volume range from about 1 to 18 L a day.
nephron.xlabel: tubule segment (1 = start, 5 = end)   |   y: % of filtered water

glomerulus.caption: Plasma is forced through the leaky capillary wall by blood pressure (about 55 mmHg), opposed by protein pull (30) and capsule pressure (15), leaving about 10 mmHg of net push and a filtration rate of about 125 mL/min. Slide the pressure.

proximal_tubule.caption: The first tube reclaims all filtered glucose, but its transporters saturate (transport maximum). In diabetes, blood glucose above about 180 mg/dL overloads them and sugar spills into urine. Slide the transport capacity.

loop_of_henle.caption: The hairpin multiplies a small 200 mOsm difference at each level into a gradient of 900 mOsm: the ascending limb pumps out salt but not water, drawing water out of the descending limb. A deeper gradient gives more concentrated urine. Slide the maximum.
loop_of_henle.xlabel: depth in the medulla   |   y: mOsm/kg

distal_tubule.caption: The distal tubule fine-tunes the filtrate. The NCC transporter reclaims 5-7% of filtered sodium and is blocked by thiazide diuretics; PTH adds calcium reabsorption; aldosterone raises sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.

collecting_duct.caption: ADH tells the collecting-duct cells to insert water channels, so water follows the salt gradient out and the urine becomes concentrated; with no ADH the urine is dilute and plentiful. Slide the ADH level.

ureters.caption: The ureters push urine toward the bladder with waves of squeezing, a few per minute, even upside down. Each wave sends a small bolus of urine along the 25-30 cm tube. Slide the rate.

bladder.caption: The bladder stretches with almost no rise in pressure up to about 300 mL (thanks to its folded, stretchy wall); first desire comes at about 150 mL and strong urgency near 400 mL. Beyond about 500 mL pressure climbs steeply. Slide the volume.

urethra.caption: Continence is a negotiation: the sphincters stay shut until the brainstem and cortex agree. Then the bladder muscle contracts and the sphincters relax together. The urethra is about 4 cm long in women and 20 cm in men.

pituitary_gland.caption: The pea-sized pituitary (about 0.5 g), under hypothalamic control, releases hormones that drive other glands (TSH to thyroid, ACTH to adrenals, FSH and LH to gonads): the "master gland". The posterior lobe stores two hypothalamic hormones, ADH and oxytocin.

thyroid.caption: Negative feedback: the pituitary raises TSH when thyroid hormone (free T4) is low, and lowers it when T4 is high. A 2-fold change in T4 makes a roughly 100-fold change in TSH, which is why TSH is such a sensitive test. Slide T4.

parathyroid_glands.caption: Four tiny glands behind the thyroid read blood calcium continuously. Falling calcium makes them pour out PTH within minutes; PTH raises calcium from bone, kidneys and (via vitamin D) the gut. Slide the calcium.

adrenal_glands.caption: Cortisol follows a daily rhythm: highest on waking (about 8 am) and lowest around midnight. Stress (slider) adds a surge from the adrenal cortex, while the medulla releases adrenaline within seconds.

pineal_gland.caption: The pineal releases melatonin in the dark, peaking at about 3 am, and bright light at night suppresses it (ordinary room light, 100-200 lux, cuts it by half or more). The time axis runs from noon to noon. Slide the evening light.
pineal_gland.xlabel: clock time (hours, 24 = midnight, 36 = noon)   |   y: pg/mL

spleen.caption: The spleen filters about 150-300 mL of blood per minute: macrophages remove old red cells (about 2 million per second) and bacteria, and its white pulp starts immune responses. It can store extra red cells and platelets.

thymus.caption: T cells learn to tell self from foreign in the thymus, which is most active in childhood and shrinks about 3% a year after that, replaced by fat. This is one reason immunity changes with age. Slide the age.

lymph_nodes.caption: About 600 nodes are scattered along the lymph vessels, like checkpoints. Germs and antigens reach waiting B and T cells here, which is why nodes swell when you are fighting an infection.

lymphatic_vessels.caption: Capillaries leak about 20 litres of fluid a day into the tissues; about 17 L return directly and about 3 L (with proteins and fat) return through the lymphatic vessels. Slide lymph function to 0 and the 3 L backs up as swelling (lymphedema).

skin.caption: The skin is a radiator: as core temperature rises, skin blood flow can climb from about 0.25 to 7 L/min (over half the cardiac output) so heat escapes; in the cold it shuts down. Slide the core temperature.

epidermis.caption: The epidermis is thinnest on the eyelids (about 0.05 mm) and thickest on the soles (up to 1.5 mm), where the outer dead layer is built up by friction. It renews itself about every month.

dermis.caption: Skin is soft at first (the coiled collagen straightens out) and then stiff, a J-shaped curve that protects against tearing. With age (higher stiffness factor) the curve steepens as the dermis loses elastin. Slide the stiffness.

hair_follicle.caption: A hair grows about 1 cm a month during its long growth phase (2-7 years), which sets its maximum length. It then rests for about 3 months before it is shed and replaced. Slide the growth duration.

sweat_gland.caption: When core temperature climbs above about 37.4 °C, sweating switches on steeply (up to 1.5 L/h, or about 3 L/h after heat acclimatization). Each litre that evaporates removes about 670 W-hours of heat. Slide acclimatization.

hypodermis.caption: Fat conducts heat poorly (thermal conductivity about 0.2 W/m·K), so a thicker layer drops the temperature more for the same heat flow: that is its insulation job, along with cushioning and storing energy. Slide the thickness and heat flow.

testes.caption: The testes make about 1,000 sperm every second, taking about 74 days per batch, at 2-4 °C below body temperature (hence the scrotum). Leydig cells make testosterone in the spaces between tubules.

ovaries.caption: The ovarian cycle runs on feedback between brain and ovary: rising estradiol triggers a short LH surge, which releases the egg (ovulation); the empty follicle then makes progesterone for about 14 days. The luteal phase stays at 14 days; the first half stretches. Slide the cycle length.

uterus.caption: The uterine lining thickens in two stages: estrogen in the first half rebuilds it from about 2 mm to 10 mm, and progesterone then makes it a receptive 12-14 mm. If no embryo arrives, hormones fall and the lining is shed (menstruation). Slide the cycle length.
